L15: # Physiology, Renal
L16: 
L17: Ogobuiro I, Tuma F.
L18: 
L19: 【5†Publication Details】
L20: ## Introduction
L21: The renal system consists of the kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. The system filters approximately 200 L of fluid daily from the renal circulation, allowing toxins, metabolic waste products, and excess ions to be excreted while essential substances are retained in the blood. The kidneys regulate plasma osmolarity by modulating the amount of water, solutes, and electrolytes in the blood.
L22: These organs maintain long-term acid-base balance and produce erythropoietin, which stimulates red blood cell production. The kidneys also secrete renin to regulate blood pressure and convert vitamin D to its active form. This article reviews renal development, urine production and excretion, and the clinical significance of the renal system.
L23: ## Development
L24: Three sets of kidneys develop consecutively from the urogenital ridges, and the final set persists as the adult kidneys. The first renal tubular system is the pronephros. The pronephros develops during the fourth week of embryonic development but rapidly degenerates as the mesonephros forms. The mesonephric kidneys subsequently regress as the metanephros develops, although portions of the mesonephric ducts are incorporated into the male reproductive system.
L25: The metanephros begins developing during the fifth week of embryonic development through formation of the ureteric buds. As the ureteric buds develop, they induce nephron formation.【6†[1]】 The distal portions of the ureteric buds develop into the renal pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts, whereas the proximal portions form the ureters.【6†[1]】【7†[2]】 The cloaca divides to form the anorectal canal and urogenital sinus.
L26: The anorectal canal gives rise to the rectum and upper anal canal, whereas the urogenital sinus contributes to the formation of the urinary bladder and urethra.By the third month of fetal development, the metanephric kidneys can excrete urine into the amniotic fluid.【8†[3]】
L27: ## Mechanism
L28: 
L29: Glomerular Filtration
L30: Glomerular filtration is the initial process in urine production. Hydrostatic pressure passively moves fluid and solutes through the glomerular filtration membrane without requiring energy.
L31: The filtration membrane has 3 layers: the fenestrated endothelium of the glomerular capillaries, which permits plasma components other than blood cells to pass; the glomerular basement membrane, a negatively charged physical barrier that restricts protein filtration; and the filtration slits between podocyte foot processes, which provide additional selective filtration.
L32: The balance between outward and inward pressures across the glomerular capillaries determines the amount of water and solutes that cross the filtration membrane. Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is the principal filtration force and measures approximately 55 mm Hg. Capsular colloid osmotic pressure represents another potential filtration force but is normally 0 mm Hg because proteins are generally absent from the capsular space.
L33: Conversely, capsular hydrostatic pressure and glomerular capillary colloid osmotic pressure oppose filtration. The balance of these forces produces the net filtration pressure, which substantially influences the glomerular filtration rate.【9†[4]】
L34: The glomerular filtration rate is the volume of fluid filtered each minute and depends on net filtration pressure, the total surface area available for filtration, and filtration membrane permeability. The reference glomerular filtration rate is approximately 120 to 125 mL/min. Intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms regulate the glomerular filtration rate. Intrinsic regulation adjusts renal vascular resistance through myogenic and tubuloglomerular feedback mechanisms.
L35: The myogenic mechanism maintains the glomerular filtration rate by constricting the afferent arteriole when increased blood pressure stretches vascular smooth muscle. When pressure within the afferent arteriole decreases, vascular smooth muscle relaxes, allowing greater blood flow into the glomerulus. Tubuloglomerular feedback regulates the glomerular filtration rate by sensing the sodium chloride concentration within the tubular fluid.
L36: Macula densa cells detect sodium chloride delivery near the thick ascending limb of the nephron loop.【10†[5]】 Elevated blood pressure increases the glomerular filtration rate and decreases the time available for sodium reabsorption, resulting in a higher tubular sodium chloride concentration. Macula densa cells respond by releasing vasoconstrictive mediators that constrict the afferent arteriole and reduce renal blood flow.
L37: Conversely, reduced pressure permits greater sodium reabsorption, decreases tubular sodium chloride delivery, and limits the release of vasoconstrictive mediators by the macula densa cells.【11†[6]】【12†[7]】
L38: Extrinsic regulation maintains the glomerular filtration rate and systemic blood pressure through the sympathetic nervous system and renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. A substantial decrease in extracellular fluid volume stimulates the release of norepinephrine and epinephrine, causing renal vasoconstriction and reducing renal blood flow and the glomerular filtration rate. Decreased blood pressure activates the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system through 3 principal mechanisms.
L39: First, β1-adrenergic receptor activation stimulates renin release from juxtaglomerular granular cells. Second, macula densa cells detect reduced sodium chloride delivery during decreased renal blood flow and signal granular cells to release renin. Third, intrarenal baroreceptors near the granular cells detect decreased arteriolar wall tension and further stimulate renin release, thereby contributing to regulation of glomerular filtration.【11†[6]】
L40: Tubular Reabsorption
L41: The 4 tubular segments have distinct reabsorptive properties. The proximal convoluted tubule has the greatest reabsorptive capacity. Under physiologic conditions, this segment reabsorbs nearly all filtered glucose and amino acids and approximately 65% of filtered sodium and water. Proximal convoluted tubule cells reabsorb sodium through primary active transport by the basolateral sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase.
L42: Glucose, amino acids, and vitamins undergo sodium-dependent secondary active transport, whereas electrochemical gradients drive passive paracellular diffusion. Water follows solute reabsorption through osmosis. Lipid-soluble substances undergo passive diffusion along concentration gradients created by water reabsorption. Urea is also reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule through passive paracellular diffusion along its concentration gradient.【13†[8]】
L43: Filtrate that is not reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule enters the nephron loop, which consists of descending and ascending limbs. The descending limb reabsorbs water through osmosis because of its high aquaporin expression but has limited solute permeability. Conversely, the ascending limb is impermeable to water.
L44: Sodium moves passively along its concentration gradient in the thin ascending limb, whereas the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter reabsorbs these ions in the thick ascending limb. Basolateral sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase maintains the ionic gradient required for cotransporter function. Calcium and magnesium also undergo passive paracellular reabsorption in the ascending limb, driven by the electrochemical gradient.【14†[9]】
L45: The distal convoluted tubule is the next nephron segment involved in reabsorption. Basolateral sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase provides primary active sodium transport, whereas apical sodium-chloride cotransporters and ion channels mediate secondary active transport. Aldosterone regulates sodium reabsorption in the distal portion of this segment. Calcium enters cells through apical channels under the influence of parathyroid hormone.
L46: Aldosterone acts on cells in the late distal convoluted tubule to increase the synthesis and retention of apical sodium and potassium channels and basolateral sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase.【13†[8]】
L47: The collecting tubule follows the distal convoluted tubule and performs the final adjustments in tubular reabsorption. Sodium reabsorption occurs through apical channels and basolateral sodium-potassium adenosine triphosphatase under aldosterone regulation. Water permeability varies according to antidiuretic hormone activity, allowing the collecting tubule to regulate final urine concentration.
L48: Additional ion transport mechanisms in this segment contribute to potassium, hydrogen ion, and acid-base regulation.【15†[10]】
L49: Tubular Secretion
L50: Tubular secretion removes substances such as medications and metabolites that are bound to plasma proteins and therefore filtered poorly at the glomerulus. This process also eliminates undesirable substances that may have been passively reabsorbed, including urea and uric acid. Aldosterone regulates potassium secretion in the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. When blood pH decreases below the reference range, renal tubular cells increase hydrogen ion secretion.
L51: Conversely, alkalemia promotes bicarbonate excretion and chloride conservation. The renal tubules also secrete creatinine, ammonia, and numerous organic acids and bases.【16†[11]】
L52: Storage of Urine
L53: Once urine production is complete, urine travels through the ureters to the urinary bladder for storage. The human body has 2 ureters, 1 on each side. Each ureter is a slender tube with a 3-layered wall consisting of a mucosa lined by transitional epithelium, a muscularis composed of inner longitudinal and outer circular smooth muscle layers, and an adventitia composed of fibrous connective tissue.
L54: As urine enters a ureter, smooth muscle stretching initiates peristaltic contractions that propel urine toward the bladder.【17†[12]】 The oblique insertion of the ureters into the posterior bladder wall prevents urinary reflux. Once urine enters the bladder, the organ's specialized anatomy permits efficient storage. The bladder is a muscular reservoir with 3 principal wall layers.
L55: These layers resemble those of the ureter, although the bladder muscularis contains inner and outer longitudinal layers and a middle circular layer. Collectively, these smooth muscle fibers form the detrusor muscle. Bladder distensibility permits a maximum capacity of approximately 1000 mL, although the usual functional capacity is 300 to 400 mL.【18†[13]】 The bladder has 3 openings within a smooth triangular region called the trigone.
L56: Two openings receive the distal ureters, and the third forms the internal urethral orifice.
L57: The urethra is a thin-walled muscular tube that drains urine from the bladder. Its mucosal lining consists primarily of pseudostratified columnar epithelium, although transitional epithelium lines the proximal portion. Thickening of smooth muscle at the bladder-urethra junction forms the internal urethral sphincter, which is controlled by the autonomic nervous system. The male urethra also transports semen.
L58: In men, the urethra measures approximately 22.3 cm and consists of prostatic, membranous, and spongy regions.【19†[14]】 In women, the urethra measures approximately 3.8 to 5.1 cm, and the external urethral orifice lies anterior to the vaginal opening and posterior to the clitoris.【20†[15]】
L59: Micturition Process
L60: Micturition involves contraction of the detrusor muscle and relaxation of the internal and external urethral sphincters. Neural control of this process changes with development. In children younger than 3 years, a spinal reflex primarily coordinates micturition. Urine accumulation stretches the bladder wall and activates mechanoreceptors within the detrusor muscle.
L61: Visceral afferent signals travel to the sacral spinal cord, where interneurons stimulate parasympathetic neurons and inhibit sympathetic activity. These afferent signals also decrease somatic efferent activity that normally maintains contraction of the external urethral sphincter, thereby permitting reflexive urination.
L62: After approximately 3 years of age, supraspinal control develops and permits voluntary regulation of the external urethral sphincter.【21†[16]】 A high bladder volume activates the pontine micturition center, which increases parasympathetic activity, inhibits sympathetic activity, and produces awareness of bladder fullness. These responses contract the detrusor muscle and relax the internal urethral sphincter, while voluntary relaxation of the external urethral sphincter permits voiding.
L63: Conversely, a low bladder volume activates the pontine storage center, which increases sympathetic and somatic activity and suppresses parasympathetic activity, thereby promoting urinary storage.【22†[17]】
L64: ## Clinical Significance
L65: 
L66: Renal system disorders have diverse clinical presentations. The following sections discuss emphysematous urinary tract infections, chronic kidney disease, nephrolithiasis, and urinary incontinence in men and women.
L67: 
L68: Emphysematous Urinary Tract Infections
L69: An emphysematous urinary tract infection is an infection of the upper or lower urinary tract characterized by gas formation.
L70: Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae commonly cause these infections, although Proteus, Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, and Clostridium organisms and Candida spp may also be causative pathogens.【23†[18]】 Common risk factors include diabetes and urinary tract obstruction.【24†[19]】 Emphysematous infections may manifest as cystitis, pyelitis, or pyelonephritis, with clinical features including fever, chills, flank or abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
L71: Laboratory testing may reveal an elevated serum creatinine level, pyuria, leukocytosis, and hyperglycemia. Radiography or CT can establish the diagnosis by demonstrating gas within the renal parenchyma, bladder, or surrounding tissues.【24†[19]】 Treatment usually involves systemic antimicrobial therapy.【24†[19]】【25†[20]】 Percutaneous drainage may be necessary for emphysematous pyelonephritis.
L72: Chronic kidney disease is common, affecting approximately 16.8% of the US population.【26†[21]】 Chronic kidney disease is defined by kidney damage, including urinary protein excretion greater than 29 mg/d, or a glomerular filtration rate less than 60 mL/min/1.73 m² for at least 3 months. The condition is classified according to 6 glomerular filtration rate categories and 3 proteinuria categories. Clinical manifestations include edema and hypertension, although some patients remain asymptomatic.
L73: Laboratory testing is essential for diagnosis, and common findings include elevated serum creatinine and blood urea nitrogen levels. Additional findings may include hyperphosphatemia, hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, elevated parathyroid hormone levels, and metabolic acidosis. When chronic kidney disease is suspected, renal ultrasonography, urinalysis with microscopy, and measurement of the urinary protein-to-creatinine ratio are indicated.
L74: Renal ultrasonography helps exclude urinary tract obstruction.【27†[22]】 Urinalysis with microscopy may identify findings suggestive of glomerulonephritis, including proteinuria, red blood cell casts, or dysmorphic red blood cells. Sterile pyuria may suggest interstitial nephritis. When initial testing does not identify the cause, further evaluation for renovascular disease may be appropriate.
L75: Kidney biopsy may be indicated when the diagnosis remains uncertain, and patients with advanced disease require evaluation for renal replacement therapy.【28†[23]】 Treatment of chronic kidney disease includes addressing reversible causes, slowing disease progression, treating complications of kidney failure, adjusting medication dosages, and educating patients about the disease and the potential need for renal replacement therapy.【29†[24]】【30†[25]】
L76: Nephrolithiasis
L77: Nephrolithiasis is a common renal disorder characterized by crystallized calcium, magnesium, cystine, or uric acid within the urinary tract.
L78: Calcium stones account for approximately 80% of cases and occur primarily as calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate stones, with calcium oxalate being the most common type.【31†[26]】【32†[27]】 Risk factors include a diet high in oxalate, a personal or family history of nephrolithiasis, recurrent urinary tract infection, and increased enteric oxalate absorption associated with gastric bypass procedures, other bariatric surgical procedures, or short bowel syndrome.【33†[28]】【34†[29]】 Approximately 70% of patients with nephrolithiasis are asymptomatic.【35†[30]】 The most common symptomatic presentation is waxing and waning unilateral flank pain occurring in waves that last 20 to 60 min.
L79: Hematuria is also common. Alternative diagnoses should be considered during evaluation. Pyelonephritis may also cause flank pain but is more commonly accompanied by fever, which is usually absent in uncomplicated nephrolithiasis. Ectopic pregnancy may mimic renal colic, and renal and pelvic ultrasonography can help distinguish these conditions.【36†[31]】 When a symptomatic ureteral stone is suspected, noncontrast renal CT is generally indicated, and analgesic treatment should begin promptly.
L80: Urosepsis requires emergency urinary tract decompression. In the absence of urosepsis, treatment is guided by stone size. Observation, symptomatic treatment, an α-blocker, and urine straining may be appropriate for patients with stones smaller than 10 mm. Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy or ureteroscopy may benefit patients with stones larger than 10 mm.【37†[32]】
L81: Urinary Incontinence in Men
L82: Urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine and is classified as urgency, stress, mixed, or overflow incontinence caused by incomplete bladder emptying. The causes of urinary incontinence differ between men and women, although some risk factors overlap. Among men older than 65 years, 11% to 34% experience urinary incontinence.【38†[33]】 Risk factors include older age, prostate disease, a history of urinary tract infection, neurologic disease, and diabetes.
L83: The mechanisms underlying urgency incontinence remain incompletely understood, although involuntary detrusor contractions are commonly present. Stress urinary incontinence in men usually results from impaired urethral sphincter function and commonly occurs after prostate surgical procedures, pelvic trauma, or neurologic disease.【39†[34]】 Mixed incontinence combines features of stress and urgency incontinence.
L84: Overflow incontinence results from impaired detrusor contractility, bladder outlet obstruction, or both. Nocturnal enuresis may occur when pelvic floor relaxation and a full bladder contribute to leakage during sleep.
L85: Treatment of urinary incontinence usually begins with lifestyle interventions, including dietary modification, weight loss, and pelvic floor muscle exercises. If these interventions do not improve symptoms, pharmacologic therapy may be initiated according to the underlying incontinence type.
L86: Treatment options include α-blockers, antimuscarinic agents, β3-adrenergic agonists, and duloxetine.【40†[35]】【41†[36]】 Patients with persistent symptoms despite conservative and pharmacologic treatment may require procedures such as percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sacral nerve stimulation, botulinum toxin injection, transurethral bulking agent injection, perineal slings, or placement of an artificial urinary sphincter.【42†[37]】【43†[38]】【44†[39]】
L87: Urinary Incontinence in Women
L88: Approximately 50% of adult women experience urinary incontinence.【45†[40]】 Common risk factors in women include older age, obesity, parity, and mode of delivery. Stress incontinence is the most common type of urinary incontinence among women aged 45 to 49 years.【46†[41]】 Urethral hypermobility is one mechanism of stress incontinence and commonly results from inadequate support of the urethra and bladder neck by the pelvic floor musculature and vaginal connective tissues after vaginal delivery.
L89: Intrinsic sphincter deficiency is another cause and frequently develops after multiple pelvic or incontinence surgical procedures.【47†[42]】 Urgency incontinence commonly affects older women and is associated with detrusor overactivity.【48†[43]】 Overflow incontinence in women results from detrusor underactivity, bladder outlet obstruction, or both.
L90: Detrusor contractility decreases with age, and reduced estrogen levels may contribute.【49†[44]】 In women, bladder outlet obstruction may result from uterine fibroids or advanced pelvic organ prolapse. Treatment of urinary incontinence in women also begins with lifestyle and behavioral interventions, followed by pharmacologic therapy when indicated. Surgical treatment may be necessary for persistent or anatomically correctable disease.
